turns.response_html:
...stuck in a defensive feedback loop.

When rejection or heartbreak stops being an event and turns into core identity trauma, people usually adapt in one of two ways: they either turn completely inward into cynicism and chronic isolation, or they outsource their grief to dogmatic subcultures that promise simple explanations for why the game was "rigged" to begin with.

The zero-sum narrative—that romance is a tournament where a tiny fraction "wins" and everyone else is discarded—is amplified heavily by modern dating mechanics and online echo chambers. When someone is already hurting, those frameworks offer a seductive kind of comfort: it hurts less to believe a system is fundamentally broken and impossible than to sit with the vulnerability and grief of unreciprocated effort.

The real downstream crisis isn't just the initial heartbreak; it’s the calcification that follows:

  • Preemptive armor: People stop entering interactions as open human beings and start entering them with their shields raised, constantly looking for proof that they are about to be burned again.
  • Loss of agency: Viewing romance purely as a meat-grinder where 50 people lose removes personal growth from the equation, replacing genuine self-discovery with fatalism.
  • Radicalized resentment: Online communities often exploit that specific wound, turning normal human longing into grievance, hostility, or chronic emotional detachment.

The hardest part of the human side of this is that learning to bounce back requires tolerating the risk of feeling that pain again. When people lack healthy support networks or emotional tools to process that grief, the armor they build to protect themselves eventually becomes the very cage that keeps them isolated.
